Mōḍi inscription (Jayavarman II time): a ruler who put a Yadu king to flight read as Devapāla, who made a treaty with the Yādava Sīṅhaṇa (1210-1247).
Table of donations of villages, land and houses to deities (Ekalladēva, Vaidyanātha, Ajayēśvara) in a late Paramāra grant at Mōḍi: general evidence for temple endowments.
Inscription reveals Chāduri as Chief Minister of Jayavarman; Arisimha grandson of Rājaputra Gōvinda otherwise unknown.

items.note: Edition history of the Māndhātā copper-plate (Vikrama 1317) of Jayavarman II: edited by Kielhorn in Epigraphia Indica IX, plates now in Central Museum, Nagpur.
refs: Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica IX, pp. 117 ff.

items.note: Garuda engraved on the plate as the emblem of the Paramāra royal house, described in detail (four hands, snake, bearded face).
Characters are Nāgari showing a transitional stage in letter forms (i, e, k, th, bh, ś) in a Paramāra grant.
Language of the Paramāra charter is almost faultless Sanskrit, composed in verse apart from the grant portion.
Plates of Jayavarmadeva, younger brother of Jaitugideva; cite the genealogy from Bhōja to Dēvapāla; Dēvapāla succeeded by Jaitugi, then Jayavarman.
Grant issued from Manḍapa-durga; date V.S. 1317 corresponds to Sunday 7 November 1260 A.C.
Donees named with śarman suffix; the king's pratihāra Gāngadēva of high status deputed to make the grant after bathing at a confluence.
Political situation of the time: Iltutmish captured the fort of Bhilsā (modern Vidishā) in 1233-34, later Muslim and Yādava/Vāghelā attacks, possibly prompting the Paramāras to resort to Māndū.
